en: The national flower sampaguita releases its strongest fragrance at night to attract pollinating moths.
Ifugao farmers use the muyong system, planting trees above rice terraces to naturally filter irrigation water and prevent soil erosion.
During the Pahiyas Festival, locals decorate houses with kiping, which are vibrant leaf-shaped wafers made from ground rice and natural food coloring.
National Scientist Ramon Barba discovered that spraying mango trees with potassium nitrate induces them to flower during the dry season.
The national bird, the Philippine eagle, uses its distinct dark crest to communicate and relies on tall dipterocarp trees for nesting.
The national animal, the carabao, cools itself by wallowing in mud because it lacks sufficient sweat glands to regulate body temperature.
The T'boli people weave t'nalak cloth from abaca fibers, using natural dyes extracted from local roots, leaves, and bark.
Palawan's Puerto Princesa Underground River, a national treasure, features a cave system where tidal seawater visibly mixes with freshwater river flow.
During the Ati-Atihan festival in Kalibo, participants paint their skin with black soot from burned coconut husks to honor the Santo Niño.
The traditional bayanihan practice is possible because houses built from light bamboo and dried nipa palm are physically lightweight enough to carry.
The Philippine Clean Air Act mandates the use of smokestack filters in factories to reduce visible air pollution in Metro Manila.
During his exile in Dapitan, hero Jose Rizal established a water system by building a stone dam to provide clean water to the town.
